--- title: Think Bayes 🤔 subtitle: A very short introduction to Bayesian updating author: "Nelson Amaya" description: "Toss a globe, count the water, and watch a probability distribution learn. A gentle first contact with Bayesian inference, animated with the tools from session 5." categories: - statistics - probability - bayes date: "2026-07-05" date-modified: last-modified order: 6 level: Advanced duration: 60 min track: Think with data prerequisites: "Earning the arrow" image: bayes_globe.png format: live-html engine: knitr webr: packages: - ggplot2 aliases: - /sessions_workshop/13-bayes/bayes.html - /sessions_thinking/05-bayes/05-bayes.html citation: url: https://nelsonamayad.github.io/R4DEV/sessions_thinking/06-bayes/06-bayes --- ::: {.cell} ::: > *"It appears to be a quite general principle that, whenever there is a randomized way of doing something, then there is a nonrandomized way that delivers better performance but requires more thought."*
--E.T. Jaynes ::: {.lesson-info} **Level:** Advanced  ·  **Time:** ~60 min  ·  **Prerequisites:** Earning the arrow  ·  **Tools:** R running live in your browser (webR) -- no installation needed ::: ## You will learn to - Update a prior belief into a posterior, one observation at a time. - Distinguish a Bayesian posterior from a frequentist confidence interval. - Watch a probability distribution learn, animated, as data arrives. - Run and modify live R code directly in the browser via webR. ## Part I: Why Bayes? Every statistics course you took taught you to ask: *how surprising is my data, assuming some hypothesis is true?* Bayesian analysis asks the question you actually care about, in the direction you actually care about: **given the data I saw, what should I now believe?** The machinery is one line --Bayes' theorem-- and one discipline: beliefs are *distributions*, not numbers, and data doesn't replace them, it **updates** them. ### What proportion of the Earth is water? The classic teaching example, from Richard McElreath's [*Statistical Rethinking*](https://xcelab.net/rm/)[^1]: toss an inflatable globe in the air, catch it, and write down whether your index finger landed on **W**ater or **L**and. Each toss is a noisy observation of one number: $p$, the true proportion of the Earth covered by water (about 0.71, but pretend you don't know). [^1]: The best statistics book you will ever read, and the source of this example. The lectures are [free on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@rmcelreath). Nine tosses give us `W L W W W L W L W` --six waters. What should we believe about $p$? We compute it with a **grid approximation**: try every candidate value of $p$, score how well each explains the data, and weigh by what we believed before. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) tosses <- c("W","L","W","W","W","L","W","L","W") # <1> globe_posterior <- tibble(p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 200)) |> # <2> dplyr::mutate( prior = 1, # <3> likelihood = dbinom(sum(tosses == "W"), size = length(tosses), prob = p), # <4> posterior = likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior) # <5> ) globe_posterior |> ggplot(aes(x = p, y = posterior)) + geom_area(fill = "#226F7F", alpha = 0.7) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.71, linetype = "dashed", color = "#F75431") + # <6> labs(title = "What we believe after 9 tosses", subtitle = "Dashed line: the true proportion of water on Earth", x = "Candidate proportion of water (p)", y = NULL) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06-bayes_files/figure-html/6.grid-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 1. Our data: nine catches, six fingers on water. 2. The "grid": 200 candidate values for $p$ between 0 (all land) and 1 (all water). 3. A **flat prior**: before tossing, we pretend every proportion is equally plausible. Priors can --and usually should-- know more than this. 4. The **likelihood**: for each candidate $p$, the probability of seeing 6 waters in 9 tosses. Plain old `dbinom()` --the probability sibling of the `rbinom()` that tossed coins in session 5. 5. **Bayes' theorem**, literally typed out: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The division just makes it sum to one. 6. We never told the code the answer --look where the belief piles up anyway. Because the posterior is a distribution *over $p$ itself*, you can ask it questions directly. How sure are we, after nine tosses, that the Earth is mostly water? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} globe_posterior |> dplyr::summarise(prob_mostly_water = sum(posterior[p > 0.5])) # <1> ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 prob_mostly_water 1 0.828 ``` ::: ::: 1. Add up the posterior over every candidate $p$ above one half --a probability statement about the parameter, read straight off the distribution. That one line is the difference from the frequentist tools of [There is only one test](/sessions_thinking/02-inference/02-inference.qmd). A 95% confidence interval is a promise about the *procedure*: build intervals this way forever and 95% of them catch the truth. It says nothing about the probability that $p$ sits inside *this* interval. A posterior says exactly that, given this prior and these data. With a flat prior and plenty of data the two often land on similar numbers, but they answer different questions --and only the posterior answers the one people actually ask. ### Watch the learning happen A posterior is not a verdict, it is a *running belief* --so let's animate it updating toss by toss, with the exact `gganimate` tools from session 5. Frame $n$ shows what we believe after the first $n$ tosses: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gganimate) update_frames <- purrr::map_df(0:length(tosses), \(n) { # <7> tibble(p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 200)) |> dplyr::mutate( posterior = dbinom(sum(tosses[seq_len(n)] == "W"), size = n, prob = p), posterior = posterior / sum(posterior), n_tosses = n, label = ifelse(n == 0, "Before any data (the prior)", paste0("After ", n, " tosses: ", paste(tosses[seq_len(n)], collapse = " "))) ) }) update_frames |> ggplot(aes(x = p, y = posterior)) + geom_area(fill = "#226F7F", alpha = 0.7) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.71, linetype = "dashed", color = "#F75431") + labs(title = "{closest_state}", # <8> x = "Proportion of water (p)", y = NULL) + theme_classic() + gganimate::transition_states(label, transition_length = 2, state_length = 3, wrap = FALSE) + # <8> gganimate::ease_aes("cubic-in-out") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bayesian updating, one toss at a time](06-bayes_files/figure-html/6.updating-anim-1.gif) ::: ::: 7. For each $n$ from 0 to 9, we recompute the posterior using only the first $n$ tosses --ten snapshots of a mind changing. 8. `transition_states()` from session 5, nothing new. Watch how the first W rules out $p = 0$ *completely*, and how each toss reshapes --but never erases-- what came before. ## Part II: Your turn to believe The window below runs R **in your browser**. Change the prior --make it stubborn (`p^10`), sceptical of water (`(1-p)^3`), or opinionated like a geographer (`dbeta(p, 7, 3)`)-- and watch how much (or little) the same 9 tosses can teach different minds. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 200) prior <- rep(1, 200) # <- change me! likelihood <- dbinom(6, size = 9, prob = p) posterior <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior) plot(p, posterior, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#226F7F", main = "Prior (grey) vs posterior (teal)", xlab = "Proportion of water", ylab = "") lines(p, prior / sum(prior), lwd = 2, col = "grey60") abline(v = 0.71, lty = 2, col = "#F75431") ``` ::: ::: callout-tip ## Play more This repo ships a small Shiny simulator with sliders for the prior and the data --break your intuitions at will. It's live below, or run it yourself with `shiny::runApp("shiny/BayesApp")` from the project. ::: ::: column-screen-inset ::: ## Where next This was the whole idea of Bayes in one session; the rest is craft. When you are ready: - [**Statistical Rethinking**](https://xcelab.net/rm/) (McElreath) --start here, no contest. R code for everything. - [**Bayes Rules!**](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/) --free online, gentler on-ramp, tidyverse throughout. - [**`brms`**](https://paul-buerkner.github.io/brms/) --when you want real models: multilevel regression with `lm()`-like syntax, Stan under the hood. - [**`bayesplot`**](https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/) --diagnostics and posterior visualisations that match what you learned in session 2. ## 🏗 Practice 6: Update yourself {.unnumbered} The browser window above is enough for the Basic tier; the rest needs your own R session (and `brms` for the Advanced one). ::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"} # Basic - Re-run the grid approximation with 100 tosses (72 W). What happened to the width of the posterior? Why? - In the browser window above, find a prior strong enough that 9 tosses barely move it. How much data does it take to overwhelm it? ::: ::: {.callout-important icon="false" collapse="true"} # Intermediate - Animate the 100-toss updating. At what point does the animation get boring? That boredom has a name: *convergence* - The globe example has one parameter. Write down --just on paper-- what the grid would look like for **two** parameters. Now you know why MCMC exists ::: ::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"} # Advanced - Fit the globe model with real MCMC in your own R session: `brms::brm(W | trials(N) ~ 1, family = binomial, data = tibble::tibble(W = 6, N = 9))`. Convert the intercept back to a proportion with `plogis()` and compare the posterior to your grid approximation. Where do they differ, and why? (Hint: brms puts its default prior on the log-odds scale, not on the proportion.) - Pick a question from your own work where you already hold a belief (a conversion rate, a share, a success rate). Write your prior as a Beta distribution *before* looking at new data, update it with the data, and report how much the data moved you. ::: ## Key takeaways - Bayesian updating turns a prior belief into a posterior by multiplying in the likelihood of each new observation. - Grid approximation makes the whole process visible: the posterior is just a distribution getting reshaped, one data point at a time. - More data narrows the posterior and gradually overwhelms even a strong prior. - A Bayesian posterior and a frequentist confidence interval answer different questions, even when the numbers look similar. ::: {.continue-learning} [← Previous: Earning the arrow](/sessions_thinking/05-designs/05-designs.qmd) [Track overview: Think with data →](/learn/thinking.qmd) [Explore another track: Build with R →](/learn/build-with-r.qmd) :::
